A rainy December evening. The trattoria is closed. Graziella takes out an old album and calls Matei over to see it.
Come, Matei, sit down. I'll show you my family.
What a lovely album! Who's this lady with the hat?
That's my mother, Lucia. And this man with the moustache is my father, Renzo. They opened the trattoria in 1950.
So the trattoria belonged to your parents!
Yes, and before that, in my grandparents' time, it was a carpenter's workshop. Look, this is my wedding photo.
How young you were! And is this your husband?
Yes, my Aldo. We got married in 1975 at Santo Spirito. He died ten years ago.
Grandma, show him the photo of Dad when he was little! With the big ears!
Here it is. This is my son Marco, at eight. See, Pietro? His ears are just like yours.
That's not true! Mine are smaller!
And your parents, Pietro, where do they live?
In Milan. They work a lot, so I stay with Grandma during the week. Their flat is small, ours is nicer.
And you, Matei? Do you have a photo of your family?
Yes, on my phone. Here's my sister Ilinca, my parents and our dog, Lupu. In two weeks I'll see them all!
Three vowels in a row are all pronounced, in one gliding syllable: MIEI = "myay", TUOI = "twoy".
GLI = a soft "ly", with the tongue against the roof of the mouth: MO-glie = "mo-lye", FI-glio = "fee-lyo".
ZZ in "nozze" is a long "ts": NOT-TSE.
The double "ff": BAF-FI, with the "f" held longer.
In Italian the possessive usually comes BEFORE the noun and almost always has an article: "il mio libro" (my book, literally "the my book"). It agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner.
"Loro" never changes: il loro cane, la loro casa, i loro figli. Only the article changes.
"Suo / sua" means both "his" and "her" — it agrees with the object, not with the person. Context tells you who the owner is:
A typical mistake for Romanians: "Giulia e il sua cane". No! "Cane" is masculine → "il suo cane", even though Giulia is a woman.
"Suo / Sua" is also used for "Lei" (the polite form): "Signora, questa è la Sua borsa?" = "Madam, is this your bag?"

Exception: "loro" always keeps the article: "il loro padre", "la loro figlia".
"Nipote" means both grandchild and nephew / niece. "I genitori" = parents; "i parenti" = relatives (not parents!).

If you can use these eight verbs without hesitating, you can hold a simple conversation about yourself, your family, your routine and what you did yesterday. That is exactly the A1 level.

On the twenty-seventh of December Matei writes Giulia a long email. In Italian, of course: it's his holiday homework.
"Dear Giulia, I've been in Sibiu for five days. My plane arrived two hours late because of the snow, but my father waited for me at the airport with a thermos of hot tea.
It's incredibly cold here: minus twelve degrees! The town is white and the Great Square is full of lights and stalls. Every evening we drink mulled wine at the Christmas market.
On Christmas Eve all our relatives came: my uncle and aunt from Cluj, my cousins with their children, and my grandmother, who is eighty-six and cooks better than anyone.
My mother made sarmale, which are a bit like cabbage rolls. We ate for six hours. I thought of your grandmother Assunta: our grandmothers are the same!
I brought my parents Graziella's olive oil and a panettone. I gave my sister a book of Tuscan recipes, because her birthday is on the thirtieth. She said: 'But I can't cook!' Now she has to learn.
Our old dog Lupu sleeps all day by the stove. Ilinca's cat, Tigru, on the other hand, broke two baubles on the Christmas tree. My mother says Italian cats are better behaved.
I'm happy to be home, but every day I think of Florence: the trattoria, Pietro, Michelangelo, the four o'clock macchiato. And you.
I'm coming back on the second of January. Will you pick me up at the station? This time, please, on time. A hug, Matei."
Ten minutes later Giulia's answer arrives: "Excellent, not a single mistake! Yes, I'll come. I'll be there at seven, maybe half past seven…"
Perché l'aereo di Matei è arrivato in ritardo?
Che cosa ha regalato Matei a sua sorella?
